questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the core difference between documentation and evidence?
options: Documentation explains what was designed and why; evidence proves that a control actually operated, captured at the time rather than reconstructed later
Documentation and evidence mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably
Documentation is only required for Shield features; evidence is only required for encryption
Evidence is always a screenshot, while documentation is always a written paragraph
questions.explain: Documentation shows intent and design rationale; evidence proves operation -- that a specific control actually happened, on a specific occasion or continuously, captured at the time rather than reconstructed from memory afterward.

questions.q: What does a security-focused data flow diagram need to show that a general architecture diagram typically doesn't?
options: The org's annual revenue figures
Where sensitive data enters the system, every boundary it crosses, what transforms it, and where it ultimately lands or leaves the system
Only the names of every Salesforce user in the org
The physical office locations of the development team
questions.explain: A security data flow diagram traces sensitive data's actual path and every boundary it crosses -- tying directly back to Lesson 1's boundary vocabulary -- which is what makes it useful to a reviewer or an incident responder, unlike a general systems diagram.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a data flow diagram that was accurate at launch but never updated is a liability rather than an asset?
options: Because outdated diagrams automatically violate GDPR
Because Salesforce deletes diagrams that are more than one year old
Because an inaccurate diagram actively misleads anyone who trusts it during an incident investigation, when accuracy matters most
Because diagrams have no real use in incident response regardless of accuracy
questions.explain: A stale diagram doesn't just become useless -- it actively misleads a responder who trusts it during an actual incident, which is why keeping it current needs to be a defined, ongoing responsibility rather than a one-time deliverable.

questions.q: What distinguishes a SOC 2 Type II report from a SOC 2 Type I report, per this lesson?
options: Type II only applies to companies with fewer than 50 employees
There is no real difference between the two report types
Type I requires more evidence than Type II
Type II requires evidence that controls operated consistently over an observation period (often 6-12 months), while Type I is a single point-in-time assessment
questions.explain: Type II asks for evidence spanning an observation period, showing a control operated consistently over time -- a single point-in-time screenshot or export doesn't satisfy that, which is exactly why a Type I (point-in-time) report asks a different question.

questions.q: In the Lab scenario, what would you have to tell an auditor if your access reviews happened only in informal verbal conversations with no record kept?
options: That you cannot produce evidence the reviews occurred as described, because evidence has to be something captured at the time, and a verbal conversation with no record doesn't meet that bar
That the reviews definitely satisfy SOC 2 Type II requirements since they happened
That verbal conversations are always an acceptable substitute for written evidence in any audit
That the auditor is required to accept your own recollection as sufficient proof
questions.explain: Per this lesson's distinction, evidence must be captured at the time an event happened -- an unrecorded verbal conversation, however real, isn't evidence an auditor can verify, which is exactly the gap this lesson warns architects to design against ahead of time.
